text.L1: A change can be physical or chemical. The key question is: has a new substance formed?
text.L2: In a physical change, shape, size or state changes, but no new substance forms.
text.L3: Melting ghee is physical. It is still ghee, and it becomes solid again when cooled.
text.L4: Dissolving is also physical. Sugar spreads into water, but it is still there and still has mass.
text.L5: In a chemical change, one or more new substances with different properties are formed.
text.L6: Gas bubbles, a colour change, heat or light, a new smell, or a new solid can be evidence.
text.L7: Here is a common myth: dissolved sugar has disappeared and has no mass. Not true; dissolving does not make the sugar vanish.
text.L8: Baking soda and lemon juice fizz because a new gas forms. That is a chemical change.

turns.teacherReply: Safed solid ka banna naya substance banne ka evidence hai—properties badalti hain. Ab bataiye: kya sirf dhundhla hona bhi kaafi proof hai?

move.shape: give the reason yourself in one plain line (their answer was right); one idea only: Classify everyday changes using evidence, knowing that 'can it be reversed?' is a clue but not the rule; objects first, then the symbol; point at the screen only at what the on-screen row lists; never a drawing made of characters; end with one small question that makes them USE the idea — never 'samjha?'; address them with aap forms only (aap, aapka, aapne; verbs -iye / -enge), never tum or tu
prefs: Let the child explain their reasoning fi

ask.text: Ab bataiye: kya sirf dhundhla hona bhi kaafi proof hai?

turns.teacherReply: Choices: Making curd from milk ya None; every change can be undone ya Melting butter. Kaunsa badlav ulta karke original cheez waapas nahi la sakte?

move.shape: pose the question as written, in their language; then wait; read its choices plainly; no lean in your voice toward any of them; address them with aap forms only (aap, aapka, aapne; verbs -iye / -enge), never tum or tu
prefs: Let the child explain their reasoning fi
